title: Choosing a business vehicle
subtitle: Sole trader, partnership, LLP and company compared
objectives: Compare sole trader, ordinary partnership, LLP and company across legal personality, owner liability, formation formality, and public filing obligations
Explain how tax treatment differs between fiscally transparent vehicles (sole trader, partnership, LLP) and companies subject to corporation tax

Apply a client's stated priorities — limiting personal liability, minimising cost, or preserving privacy — to recommend an appropriate business vehicle, recognising that no single vehicle is objectively best

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines a partnership and anchors the default unincorporated vehicle against which LLPs and companies are compared
Creates the LLP as a body corporate with separate legal personality but partnership-style internal flexibility and tax transparency
Governs company formation, separate legal personality, limited liability, and the public filing regime at Companies House

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can list the four vehicles and recite one fact about each. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the categories — this lesson is about matching a vehicle to a client's actual priorities, not reciting a table.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards application: expect a client scenario, not a bare definitions question.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be sure you can state, without prompting, which vehicles have separate legal personality and which don't — the rest of the lesson assumes that distinction is solid.

overview.hook: A client sits across the desk wanting to start a bakery with her brother. She asks the obvious question: 'What's the best way to set this up?' There is no single right answer — only a set of trade-offs between liability, cost, tax and privacy that depend entirely on what she cares about most. This lesson is about running that conversation properly.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The comparative framework here (legal personality, liability, formality, tax, filing) is settled; specific tax rates and thresholds change with each Budget and are not the focus of this lesson.

parts.heading: Legal personality and liability: the line that matters most
parts.voice: argumentative — states the practical stakes before the labels
body: Of everything that distinguishes these four vehicles, one question does most of the work: does the business have a legal personality separate from the people running it? A sole trader and an ordinary partnership do not — in law, the business is simply the person or people carrying it on. An LLP and a company do — each is a distinct legal person, capable of owning property, suing and being sued, and continuing to exist even as its owners change.

Separate legal personality is not an abstraction; it is the mechanism behind limited liability. Where the business is a separate person, its debts are its own debts, not the owners'. A shareholder or LLP member normally risks only what they put in. A sole trader or partner has no such shield: business debts are personal debts, recoverable against their house, savings, and other assets.

This is why the conversation with a client should start here, not with tax or paperwork. If the client's overriding concern is protecting personal assets from business risk, that single fact does most of the filtering before anything else is discussed.

components.label: Legal personality and liability at a glance
points: Sole trader — no separate legal personality; unlimited personal liability for all business debts
Ordinary partnership — no separate legal personality (Partnership Act 1890, s 1); partners are personally liable, jointly for debts
LLP — separate legal personality (Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000); members' liability normally limited to their agreed contribution
Company — separate legal personality (Companies Act 2006); shareholders' liability normally limited to unpaid amounts on their shares

interaction.prompt: A sole trader's business fails owing £40,000 to suppliers. Can the suppliers pursue the trader's personal savings and house?
options: Yes — a sole trader has no separate legal personality, so business debts are personal debts
No — a sole trader's liability is always limited to the capital invested in the business
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. With no separate legal personality, there is no line between 'business assets' and 'personal assets' for a sole trader — creditors can pursue both.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — a sole trader has no limited liability shield at all. Because the business has no legal personality of its own, its debts are simply the trader's own debts.

parts.heading: Getting started: formality and cost
parts.voice: practical — walks through what a client actually has to do
body: The four vehicles sit on a spectrum of formality. A sole trader needs almost none: registering with HMRC for self-assessment is the only real legal step, and trading can begin immediately. An ordinary partnership needs no formal registration at all to exist in law — it can arise simply from two or more people carrying on business together with a view of profit, though in practice a written partnership agreement is strongly advisable.

An LLP requires formal incorporation: registration at Companies House, at least two designated members, and an incorporation document. A company requires the same registration step, plus a constitution (articles of association), at least one director, and — for most private companies — at least one shareholder.

Cost tracks formality reasonably closely. Sole trader and partnership set-up costs are minimal beyond professional advice on the agreement itself; LLP and company incorporation carry a modest Companies House fee plus the ongoing cost of complying with filing obligations that unincorporated vehicles simply do not have.

components.definition: The formal process of registering a body (an LLP or a company) at Companies House, which brings a separate legal person into existence. Sole traders and ordinary partnerships are never 'incorporated' — they have no separate legal person to create.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact below that shows this vehicle must have been formally incorporated at Companies House.
interaction.scenarioText: Two accountants agree to set up together. They register the business at Companies House, adopt a set of articles of association, and appoint themselves as the only two directors.
tappableSpans: Two accountants agree to set up together
register the business at Companies House
adopt a set of articles of association
appoint themselves as the only two directors
interaction.correctSpan: register the business at Companies House
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the incorporating step. Adopting articles and appointing directors are things that follow incorporation — the registration itself is what brings the separate legal person into existence.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the step that creates the separate legal person itself, not the steps that follow it. Articles and director appointments happen to an already-incorporated body.

parts.heading: Tax: fiscal transparency versus corporation tax
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Sole traders, ordinary partnerships and LLPs are all fiscally transparent: the business itself pays no tax on its profits. Instead, profits are treated as the income of the individual sole trader, or are allocated to partners and LLP members, who each pay income tax (and Class 2/4 National Insurance) on their share, whether or not that share is actually drawn out of the business.

A company is different in kind, not just in rate. The company itself is a separate taxpayer and pays corporation tax on its profits. Profits only reach shareholders when the company chooses to distribute them as dividends, at which point the shareholder pays income tax on the dividend received — but retained profits, left inside the company, are not taxed again at the shareholder's hands until distributed.

This creates a genuine planning choice, not just an administrative difference: a company structure can allow profits to be retained and reinvested inside the company while paying corporation tax rather than higher-rate income tax on undrawn profits. Whether that is attractive depends entirely on the client's plans for the money — precisely the kind of client-specific question this lesson keeps returning to.

components.definition: The tax treatment under which a business's profits are taxed directly in the hands of its owners as their income, rather than the business itself being taxed as a separate entity. Applies to sole traders, partnerships and LLPs; does not apply to companies.

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order profit moves from a company to a shareholder's pocket.
items: The company pays corporation tax on that profit
The board decides to declare a dividend from remaining profit
The shareholder receives the dividend and pays income tax on it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence that makes a company fiscally opaque rather than transparent — tax is levied once at the company level, and again only if and when profit is actually distributed.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — corporation tax is charged on the company's profit before any decision is made about distributing it, and a shareholder is only taxed if and when a dividend is actually paid out.

parts.heading: Public filing: what the world gets to see
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: Privacy is often underweighted by students and overweighted, correctly, by clients. A sole trader files nothing publicly beyond their own tax return, which is not publicly accessible. An ordinary partnership is in the same position — its accounts and the terms of any partnership agreement are private, seen only by HMRC and the partners themselves.

LLPs and companies trade that privacy for the benefit of separate legal personality and limited liability. Both must file accounts, a confirmation statement, and details of their members or directors and people with significant control at Companies House, all of which are public and searchable by anyone — including competitors, journalists and prospective business partners doing due diligence.

A client who prizes confidentiality about turnover, ownership or profit margins may be surprised to learn that limited liability comes at the cost of exactly that confidentiality. This is a genuine trade-off, not a technicality, and it belongs in the advice, not just in the small print.

components.text: Every company must deliver to the registrar for each financial year a copy of its annual accounts and reports before the end of the period for filing those accounts.

interaction.prompt: Under s 441 Companies Act 2006, who is under the duty to file accounts, and with whom?
options: The company itself, with the registrar of companies (Companies House)
Each individual director personally, with HMRC
The company's auditor, with the shareholders
The company, with its bank
interaction.explanation: The duty is the company's own, owed to the registrar — this is what makes company (and LLP) accounts a public record, unlike a sole trader's or partnership's tax filings with HMRC.

parts.heading: There is no 'best' vehicle — only the right one for this client
parts.voice: Socratic — resolves the lesson by returning to the opening scenario
body: Return to the bakery client. If her main worry is that a bad batch of stock or an injured customer could wipe out her savings, an LLP or company answers that directly. If she and her brother want maximum flexibility, minimum paperwork, and don't mind shared personal risk between two people who trust each other completely, an ordinary partnership may suit them better and cost far less to run.

If cash flow is tight and profits will be drawn out and spent immediately rather than retained, the tax deferral advantage of a company evaporates — fiscal transparency may simply be simpler and cheaper. If either sibling is uncomfortable with their turnover being publicly searchable, that alone may rule out LLP or company status regardless of the liability position.

The exam (and the client meeting) rewards weighing these factors against stated priorities, not reciting a table from memory. A 'wrong' answer in this lesson is usually not a wrong fact — it's picking a vehicle that ignores what the client actually said mattered to them.

components.title: Matching a vehicle to a client's priority
components.description: A decision aid for translating a client's stated priority into a starting-point recommendation.

nodes.label: What does the client say matters most?
Protecting personal assets from business risk → LLP or company
Keeping financial affairs private → sole trader or partnership
Minimum formality and cost, trusted co-owners → sole trader or partnership
Retaining and reinvesting profit rather than drawing it → company

components.textAlternative: Start by asking what the client says matters most. If protecting personal assets from business risk is the priority, an LLP or company is the starting point. If privacy of financial affairs is the priority, a sole trader or partnership keeps that private. If minimum formality and cost with trusted co-owners is the priority, a sole trader or partnership is simplest. If retaining and reinvesting profit rather than drawing it out is the priority, a company's tax treatment is usually more attractive.

interaction.prompt: A client says her only concern is that competitors should never be able to see her turnover or profit margins. How strongly does this push against choosing an LLP or company?
interaction.explanation: Public filing at Companies House is a defining feature of LLP and company status, not an optional extra. A client whose overriding priority is confidentiality of financial information is being pushed hard towards an unincorporated vehicle, whatever the liability trade-off costs her.

testPool.prompt: A husband and wife run a market stall together with no written agreement and have never registered anything beyond self-assessment with HMRC. Does their business have legal personality separate from them?
options: No — as an unregistered arrangement it has no separate legal personality of any kind
Yes — HMRC registration automatically confers separate legal personality
Yes — but only once their combined turnover exceeds the VAT threshold
No — but it would gain separate legal personality if they wrote a partnership agreement
testPool.explanation: Neither a sole trader nor an unincorporated partnership has separate legal personality, regardless of registration with HMRC or the existence of a written agreement. Only incorporation (as an LLP or company) creates a separate legal person.

testPool.prompt: A client wants a structure where the business itself, rather than its owners personally, is capable of owning the freehold of its premises. Which vehicles can do this?
options: Only a company
An LLP or a company, but not a sole trader or ordinary partnership
Any of the four vehicles
Only an ordinary partnership
testPool.explanation: Only bodies with separate legal personality can own property in their own right. That means an LLP or a company; a sole trader and an ordinary partnership cannot, because the business is not a legal person distinct from the individuals running it.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is required to bring an ordinary partnership into legal existence?
options: Registration at Companies House
A written partnership agreement signed by all partners
Nothing beyond two or more people carrying on business together with a view of profit
Appointment of at least one designated member
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often assume 'partnership' implies paperwork because 'company' does. Under s 1(1) Partnership Act 1890, a partnership exists the moment the statutory relationship is satisfied — no registration, filing, or written agreement is required, though all three are wise practice.
testPool.explanation: A partnership can arise purely from conduct; the formal steps in the other options belong to LLPs and companies, not ordinary partnerships.

testPool.prompt: A sole trader asks her solicitor whether she must file her accounts anywhere that competitors could search. Based on the public filing regime under the Companies Act 2006, what should the solicitor advise?
options: That regime does not apply to her — as a sole trader she has no Companies House filing obligation at all
She must file abbreviated accounts only
She must file full accounts but they remain confidential to HMRC
She must file accounts within nine months of her year end
testPool.explanation: The Companies Act 2006 filing regime, including s 441, applies to companies (and by separate but parallel provision, LLPs) — not to sole traders, who have no Companies House obligations whatsoever.

testPool.prompt: A client believes that because a company pays a lower headline tax rate on profits than the top rate of income tax, a company is always the more tax-efficient choice. Which of the following best corrects this assumption?
options: Corporation tax rates are always higher than income tax rates, so the client is simply wrong
The comparison depends on whether profits are retained or extracted — extracted profits are taxed again as dividend income, which can erase the apparent advantage
Tax efficiency is irrelevant to vehicle choice and should not be discussed with clients
A company's rate advantage only applies in the first year of trading
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is treating the headline corporation tax rate as the whole answer. Because dividends are taxed again in the shareholder's hands, the real comparison depends on what the client actually plans to do with the profit — draw it out, or leave it in the business.
testPool.explanation: Fiscal transparency versus corporation tax is not simply 'which rate is lower' — it turns on the client's plans for retention versus extraction of profit.

testPool.prompt: An LLP and an ordinary partnership are often confused by clients because both have 'partnership' in common usage. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: An LLP has separate legal personality and normally limits members' liability; an ordinary partnership has neither feature
An LLP has no separate legal personality, unlike an ordinary partnership
Both are fiscally opaque and pay corporation tax
An ordinary partnership must be incorporated at Companies House, unlike an LLP
testPool.explanation: The LLP borrows the internal flexibility and tax transparency associated with 'partnership' but is, structurally, incorporated with separate legal personality and limited liability — the opposite of an ordinary partnership on both counts.

testPool.prompt: The Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 is often described as creating a hybrid vehicle. Which combination of features does it actually give an LLP?
options: Unlimited liability for members combined with public filing obligations
Separate legal personality and limited liability, combined with partnership-style internal flexibility and tax transparency
No separate legal personality, combined with corporation tax treatment
Separate legal personality but no requirement to file accounts publicly
testPool.explanation: The 'hybrid' description reflects that an LLP takes its external, corporate-style features (legal personality, limited liability, public filing) from company law, while keeping partnership-style internal governance and fiscal transparency for tax.

testPool.prompt: A trainee states that a company is always the safest choice for a new business because limited liability removes all personal risk for the owners. Why is this overstated?
options: It is not overstated — limited liability removes all personal risk once a company is formed
Directors and shareholders commonly give personal guarantees to lenders and landlords, which reintroduces personal exposure despite limited liability
Limited liability only applies to companies with more than one shareholder
Limited liability is lost automatically after the company's first year of trading
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is treating 'limited liability' as an absolute shield. In practice, banks and landlords routinely require personal guarantees from directors of small companies precisely because the company's own liability is limited — so the theoretical protection is often contracted around.
testPool.explanation: Limited liability limits liability to the company itself as a matter of law, but that protection can be — and commonly is — undermined by personal guarantees the owners choose or are required to give.

testPool.prompt: A freelance graphic designer works alone, has no employees, and wants the absolute minimum of ongoing paperwork. She is not worried about liability because she carries professional indemnity insurance. Which vehicle best fits her stated priorities?
options: Sole trader
LLP
Company
Ordinary partnership
testPool.explanation: With no co-owners, no appetite for liability protection given her insurance, and a priority on minimal formality, a sole trader is the closest fit — incorporation would add cost and filing obligations she does not want in exchange for a protection she says she doesn't need.

testPool.prompt: Three architects want to set up together. They want each of them to be shielded from personal liability for the professional negligence of the other two, and they are comfortable with public filing requirements. What should the solicitor advise?
options: An ordinary partnership, since architects traditionally practise that way
An LLP, since it offers limited liability alongside partnership-style flexibility, and they have already accepted public filing
A sole trader arrangement for each of them separately
None of the vehicles can achieve what they are asking for
testPool.explanation: An LLP is designed for exactly this professional-services scenario: it limits each member's exposure to the others' negligence (subject to their own conduct) while keeping the internal flexibility professionals often want, and the clients here have no objection to public filing.

testPool.prompt: A married couple plan to run a consultancy generating far more profit than they need to live on, intending to reinvest the surplus in growing the business for several years before drawing it out. Which factor most strongly favours a company here?
options: Companies are always cheaper to run than partnerships
Retaining profit inside a company defers income tax on that profit until it is actually distributed, unlike a fiscally transparent vehicle where it is taxed as it arises
Companies are exempt from public filing if profits are reinvested
A company is the only vehicle two people can jointly own
testPool.explanation: Because a company is fiscally opaque, undistributed profit is taxed once, at corporation tax rates, and not again until a dividend is actually paid — whereas in a fiscally transparent vehicle the couple would be taxed on the full profit as it arises, whether or not they draw it out. That deferral is the live tax reason to prefer a company on these facts.

testPool.prompt: A start-up founder tells her solicitor she is desperate to avoid ever appearing on a public register, but also wants investors to be able to buy a defined percentage shareholding with limited liability. What should the solicitor advise?
options: A company can satisfy both requirements simultaneously
These two priorities are in tension — a company (needed for the shareholding structure and limited liability) necessarily brings public filing, including a register of people with significant control
An LLP resolves the tension, since LLP members are not publicly listed
A sole trader arrangement with an informal investment side-letter resolves the tension
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming a clever structuring choice can deliver both. Public filing (including a PSC register) is a structural feature of company (and LLP) status, not a separable add-on — the founder's two priorities are genuinely in conflict, and the advice should say so honestly rather than promise both.
testPool.explanation: A defined shareholding with limited liability points firmly to a company, but that same incorporation necessarily brings public filing obligations the founder says she wants to avoid — the solicitor's job here is to flag the trade-off, not paper over it.

testPool.prompt: Two former colleagues start advising clients together, splitting fees informally, without ever discussing what legal structure they are using. One of them later denies they were ever 'partners'. Applying the Partnership Act 1890 definition, what is the most likely legal analysis?
options: No partnership exists because neither of them intended to form one
A partnership is likely to exist regardless of their intentions, because they are carrying on business in common with a view of profit
A partnership can only exist once a written agreement is signed
A partnership exists only if they registered a trading name
testPool.explanation: Section 1(1) asks only whether the statutory relationship is factually satisfied — carrying on business in common with a view of profit — not whether the parties subjectively intended or labelled it a 'partnership'. Denial after the fact does not undo a partnership that has already arisen on the facts.

testPool.prompt: A sole trader's business grows rapidly and she takes on a business partner, but neither wants the cost or filing burden of incorporation, and both are comfortable sharing personal liability given how well they know and trust each other. What vehicle now fits, and why?
options: A company, because growth always requires incorporation
An ordinary partnership, because it matches their stated tolerance for shared liability and their preference against formality and cost
An LLP, because two owners always require limited liability
A sole trader arrangement continued by one of them alone
testPool.explanation: Nothing about growth itself requires incorporation. Given their explicit comfort with shared personal liability and their preference for low cost and minimal formality, an ordinary partnership — not an LLP or company — matches their stated priorities.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating one factor — usually liability — as decisive on its own. Nearly every scenario rewards weighing liability against tax treatment, privacy, and cost together, against what the client actually said mattered to them.
